title: What firms are trying to achieve

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the objectives firms may pursue, and explain why the aim that leads differs between firms and over time.

blocks.heading: Four aims
blocks.text: Firms may pursue survival, social welfare, profit maximisation and growth, and the aim that leads changes with the firm's situation. Profit is total revenue minus total cost, and profit maximisation is the aim of making that gap as large as the firm can. Growth means expanding the firm's sales, its premises or its share of the market. Survival means keeping the firm going through a hard stretch. Social welfare means running the firm for the good of the community around it.

blocks.heading: Which aim leads, where
blocks.text: A juice processor newly opened in Oshakati may put survival first: covering its costs and keeping its customers matters more to it than the largest possible profit while its name is still unknown. A secure firm, such as an established bottler in Brazil with steady sales, may choose growth - a second line, a new warehouse - accepting a smaller profit now for bigger sales later. A bus service run for a town council may put social welfare first, keeping fares low so workers reach their jobs, and a council water utility in Namibia is set up the same way.

blocks.heading: Why a firm may choose growth
blocks.text: Growth deserves a closer look, because a firm choosing it gives up profit its owners could take out now. A firm that grows sells more and wins a larger share of its market, which makes it harder for rivals to push aside and so makes its future more secure. A bigger output may also bring the economies of scale of topic 3.5, lowering average cost so that profit per unit rises later. Oshana Bottlers, earning N$400 000 profit a year, might spend N$250 000 of it on a second line rather than pay it out to its owners: the profit paid out to its owners this year falls to N$400 000 - N$250 000 = N$150 000, in the hope that the extra sales raise profit in later years. Growth carries a risk too: if the extra sales do not come, the money has been spent and profit stays lower.

blocks.heading: When aims pull apart
blocks.text: Objectives may pull against each other. Paying workers more, keeping fares low or funding a local clinic raises the firm's costs or trims its revenue, and each such step may shrink profit. A firm choosing growth spends on expansion rather than taking profit out. A firm set on survival may accept a loss for a season to keep its customers. So a firm often trades some profit away for another aim, and which trade it makes is a judgement about its situation rather than a fixed rule.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The cost and revenue figures behind each aim are sections 3.7.1 to 3.7.4; the market setting that shapes what a firm can earn is topic 3.8, and the workers it employs are topic 3.3.
